title: Drop Scones
subtitle: Scottish griddle pancakes
excerpt: Small, thick, fluffy Scottish pancakes cooked on a dry griddle. Also called Scotch pancakes, these are quicker and more tender than a crepe, and best eaten warm from the pan with butter and jam or golden syrup.

recipe.sourceNotes: Drop scones, or Scotch pancakes, have been a Scottish staple since at least the nineteenth century, when every Scottish household had an iron girdle (griddle) kept over the fire. The name drop scone refers to the method: a spoonful of batter is dropped onto the hot griddle. Queen Elizabeth II famously served them at Balmoral to President Eisenhower in 1959 and later shared the recipe with him by letter. They are standard at Scottish breakfasts and as an afternoon treat.

content.text: The batter should be thick enough to hold its shape when dropped onto the griddle. If it spreads too much, the scones will be thin and crepe-like rather than small and fluffy. Cook over medium heat: too hot and the outside burns before the inside sets; too cool and they dry out before they colour. Flip when bubbles break the surface and the edges look set.

Whisk together the flour, sugar, and salt. Make a well in the centre. Add the eggs and half the milk and whisk from the centre outwards until smooth. Add the remaining milk gradually until the batter is thick and drops slowly from a spoon. Stir in the melted butter. Rest for 5 minutes.

Heat a griddle or heavy frying pan over medium heat. Rub lightly with a piece of kitchen paper dipped in butter. Drop tablespoons of batter onto the griddle, spaced well apart. Cook for 2 minutes until bubbles appear on the surface and the edges look set.
Flip and cook for 1 to 2 minutes more until golden. The scones should be 6 to 7 cm across. Keep warm wrapped in a clean tea towel while you cook the rest. Serve warm with butter and jam.
